442.title: An audience of one
442.hook: enough are few, enough is one, enough is none
442.howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism try to do their work well regardless of how many will see it, treating a single person, or no one, as audience enough.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the crowd, and the line was what I bring home. Did you skip one crowd that coarsens you, and what did you bring home instead? Day four hundred forty-two.

A post gets four likes and you feel faintly foolish for having shared it. A song you worked on for months gets a hundred plays. A talk you prepared for gets a half-empty room. Counting the audience is almost automatic now; there's a number under nearly everything we make. Seneca didn't have the number, but he knew the itch. Right after warning Lucilius about the crowd, he ends his seventh letter with three small sayings about how big an audience really needs to be. Today: Democritus.
screen: `FOUR LIKES.` → `A HALF-EMPTY ROOM.` → `AN AUDIENCE OF ONE.`

segments.voice: First, the setup. Seneca has just said: avoid the crowd. Lucilius might object: then what did I learn all this for, if no one will hear it? Seneca's first answer: you learned it for yourself. So Seneca gives him three sayings, like three small gifts. Second, Democritus. The old philosopher of atoms said, roughly: one person counts as much as a whole people to me, and a whole people as much as one. The size of the audience doesn't change the worth of the work. Third, the craftsman. Someone, Seneca says it's uncertain who, was asked why he took such pains over an art that very few would ever appreciate. His answer: a few are enough for me. One is enough. None is enough. Even no audience at all. The work was worth doing well for its own sake. Fourth, Epicurus. And the third gift, again from Epicurus, the founder of a rival school, writing to a friend who studied with him: I say this not for the many, but for you; we are each a big enough audience for the other. Seneca's point, gathering all three: don't let the pleasure of being praised by many pull you back into the crowd. Do your work well for the one person in front of you, or for no one, and let that be enough. Most of the good in the world is done for an audience of one: a meal for a sick friend, a letter, a careful repair, a child's question answered properly. Nobody counts those. They count anyway.
screen: `WHO WILL SEE MY WORK?` · `DEMOCRITUS: ONE IS A WHOLE PEOPLE.` · `A FEW, ONE, EVEN NONE IS ENOUGH.` · `EPICURUS: AUDIENCE ENOUGH.` · then, large: `ONE IS ENOUGH.`

segments.voice: Think of one person who will benefit from something you do today. A coworker who needs your notes. A parent who'd like a call. A kid who needs help with homework. A customer, a patient, a neighbor. Picture their face. Now picture doing that one thing really well, as if they were the whole audience, because they are. No one else needs to see it. Let yourself feel that this is enough. Breathe, and hold their face for a moment longer. The bell holds the time.
Democritus. The old philosopher of atoms, quoted by Seneca: one person counts as much as a whole people to me, and a whole people as much as one.
Your line: one is enough. Do one piece of good work today for one person, and don't count who else notices. Day four hundred forty-two.

screen: `DAY 442 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: ALL MINE IS WITH ME.`

443.title: All mine is with me
443.hook: Stilpo lost city, wife and children and said everything of his was still with him
443.howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism reflect on which of their goods are truly their own, character, judgment, kindness, so that losses elsewhere do not take away their footing.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Democritus. Your line was one is enough. Did you do one piece of good work for one person, without counting who noticed? Day four hundred forty-three.

A city has just fallen. The conqueror, a king called Demetrius, nicknamed the Besieger of Cities, has taken Megara. Houses are wrecked, goods carried off, families scattered. Somewhere in the ruins stands a philosopher named Stilpo, whose home is gone and whose wife and children are lost to him. The king asks him: have you lost anything? Seneca tells the story, and Stilpo's answer, in his ninth letter. Today: Stilpo.
screen: `MEGARA HAS FALLEN.` → `HAVE YOU LOST ANYTHING?` → `ALL MINE IS WITH ME.`

segments.voice: First, the answer. Stilpo told the king: I have all my goods with me. Seneca explains what he meant. Stilpo had his true goods with him, the kind no hand can seize. What was scattered, wrecked and carried off, he did not count as his own, only as things that had come to him from outside. Second, the hard part. It's fair to flinch at this story. Losing a family is not a small thing, and Seneca doesn't say it is. In the same letter he says the wise person feels their troubles, and then overcomes them. Not numb. Not untouched. Still standing. Third, the friendship twist. The surprising thing is where Seneca puts this story: in a letter about friendship. Lucilius has asked whether a person who is complete in themselves needs friends at all. Seneca says the wise person is content with themselves, and can live without friends if they must, but still wants them, very much. Not to have someone who'll sit at their bedside, but to have someone at whose bedside they can sit. Fourth, the balance. So Stilpo's line isn't a reason to love less. Read this way, it's a reason to love without fear. If what's most yours can't be taken, you can give your heart to people and things freely, knowing that even if you lose them, you won't lose yourself. In Seneca's Latin: omnia mea mecum sunt. All mine is with me.

segments.voice: Take something to write on, or just count on your fingers. List a few things that are yours in Stilpo's sense, things no fire, thief or bad day could take from you. Your honesty. Your patience, on good days. The way you keep a promise. What you've learned. The love you give, even if it isn't returned. Name three, slowly. Then hold your hands together in your lap, as if holding them, and breathe. All of this is with you, right now. The bell holds the time.
Stilpo. The philosopher in fallen Megara who told the king: I have all my goods with me, the kind no hand can seize.
Your line: you won't lose yourself. Keep your short list with you today. When something goes missing, a plan, a thing, a chance, touch the list once. Day four hundred forty-three.

444.title: As if seen
444.hook: live among people as if God saw you, speak to God as if people heard
444.carry: the private and public self become one
444.howItsDone: Some people, religious and not, try to act in private as they would before a kind and clear-eyed witness, so that their private and public lives match.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Stilpo, in fallen Megara, and your line, you won't lose yourself. Did you keep your short list of what can't be taken? Day four hundred forty-four.

Behind a closed door, where nobody will ever know, small choices get made: whether to return the extra change, whether to read the message over someone's shoulder, whether to say the unkind thing in a private chat. The person making them isn't always the one the world sees. Seneca's tenth letter is about being alone, and it ends with a sentence that closes the gap between the two versions of us from both directions. Today: Athenodorus.
screen: `WHEN THE DOOR IS CLOSED.` → `TWO SLIGHTLY DIFFERENT PEOPLE.` → `AS IF SEEN.`

segments.voice: First, a warning about being alone. Seneca tells a story about Crates, the Cynic. He saw a young man walking by himself and asked what he was doing out there alone. I'm talking with myself, the young man said. Crates answered: be careful, then, you're talking with a bad man. Solitude is only good, Seneca says, if the company inside is good. Second, the open prayer. Then Seneca passes on a saying of Athenodorus, a philosopher he quotes. You'll know you're free of your cravings, he said, when you ask God for nothing that you couldn't ask for openly, in front of everyone. Seneca notes how many people whisper prayers they'd be ashamed for others to hear. Third, the sentence. And then Seneca's own line: live among people as if God were watching; speak with God as if people were listening. Two directions. When you're with others, act as you would before the highest witness you know. When you're alone with the highest, ask only for what you'd be glad to have heard. Fourth, the witness. Seneca says God here. Listeners of any faith may hear that word in their own way, and those without one can think of the best witness they can imagine. The point is the same either way. A life lived as if seen, by someone kind and clear-eyed, doesn't need two versions. The person behind the closed door and the person in the crowd can finally be the same.
screen: `CRATES: TALKING WITH A BAD MAN.` · `ASK ONLY WHAT YOU'D ASK OPENLY.` · `LIVE AS IF GOD SAW YOU.` · `ONE PERSON, NOT TWO VERSIONS.` · then, large: `AS IF SEEN.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you've been wishing for privately, a hope you haven't said out loud. Now imagine saying it plainly in a room full of people who know you. Would you be glad for them to hear it? Don't judge the answer. Just notice whether the wish changes shape when it's said in the open. If you pray, this is Athenodorus' test: could you ask it in front of everyone? If you don't, it works on any wish. The bell holds the time.
Athenodorus. The philosopher Seneca quotes: you'll know you're free of your cravings when you ask God for nothing you couldn't ask for openly, in front of everyone.
Your line: the private and public self become one. Once today, when no one is watching, act as if someone kind and clear-eyed were. Day four hundred forty-four.

445.title: Choose a Cato
445.hook: pick someone good and live as if they were watching
445.howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism keep a chosen model in mind, a person of good character, and ask in hard moments what that person would see in their choices.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Athenodorus, one self instead of two, and your line, the private and public self become one. Did you act once, alone, as if someone kind were watching? Day four hundred forty-five.

When you're stuck on something, a hard conversation, a temptation, a choice at work, there's a question people reach for: what would she do? My grandmother. My old coach. The best boss I ever had. Some people keep a name on a bracelet for just that moment. The move is old. Yesterday Seneca said to live as if God saw you. In his eleventh letter he makes it more human and more specific, with advice he borrows, once again, from Epicurus. Today: choose a Cato.
screen: `WHAT WOULD SHE DO?` → `A NAME ON A BRACELET.` → `CHOOSE A CATO.`

segments.voice: First, the blush. The letter starts with a young friend of Lucilius who blushed while talking to Seneca. Seneca liked him for it. Blushing, he says, is natural, and no amount of wisdom removes it. Actors can fake tears or fear on stage, but they can't blush on command. Some things in us we can't control; character is about what we do with the rest. Second, the guardian. Then the advice. Epicurus, Seneca says, told his students to pick out a person of good character and keep them always before their eyes, living as if that person were watching and acting as if that person could see. A guardian, Seneca calls it, a witness you carry with you. Third, the names. Choose a Cato, Seneca says. Cato the Younger was the stern Roman Stoic who refused to bend to Julius Caesar and died rather than submit. If Cato feels too severe, Seneca adds, choose Laelius, a gentler man, a statesman known as the Wise. Choose someone whose life and words and even face have pleased you. Fourth, the ruler. Why does it work? Because, Seneca says, you can't straighten something crooked without a ruler. We need a measure outside ourselves to see where we bend. Your Cato doesn't have to be famous, or Roman, or even alive. It can be a grandmother, a saint, a teacher, a neighbor. It just has to be someone whose goodness you're sure of, and whose imagined gaze makes you stand a little straighter.
screen: `THE BLUSH NO WISDOM REMOVES.` · `KEEP A GOOD PERSON BEFORE YOU.` · `CATO, OR GENTLER LAELIUS.` · `NO STRAIGHT LINE WITHOUT A RULER.` · then, large: `CHOOSE A CATO.`

segments.voice: Let your breath settle. Now let faces come to mind, people whose goodness you trust. Living or gone. Famous or known only to you. Don't pick yet, just let them come. Then let one step forward. That's your Cato. Recall one thing you actually saw them do, or know they did: a small, straight act. Hold it up like a ruler next to one choice you're facing this week. Where does your line bend away from theirs? No scolding. Just measure. The bell holds the time.
Cato. Seneca's eleventh letter, borrowing from Epicurus: choose someone good and live as if they were watching, a ruler to straighten yourself against. Today's word.
Your line: stand a little straighter. Keep the watcher you picked with you today. At one decision, ask what they'd see, and let that be your ruler. Day four hundred forty-five.

446.title: The old plane trees
446.hook: at his country house Seneca finds the trees he planted grown old, and so is he
446.howItsDone: Readers of Seneca's twelfth letter often take it as an invitation to notice their own aging with humor and affection rather than complaint.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Cato, a good person kept before your eyes, and your line, stand a little straighter. Did your watcher come with you to one decision? Day four hundred forty-six.

Seneca goes out to his house in the country. The walls are cracking, and he scolds the man who manages the place: what are you spending the money on? The manager says, very politely, that it isn't his fault. The house is old. Seneca walks on, a little irritated, out to the plane trees by the path, and finds them bare and knotted. Has nobody been looking after these? The manager swears he's been digging and watering them. And then Seneca remembers who planted them. Today: the old plane trees.
screen: `A CRACKING COUNTRY HOUSE.` → `BARE, KNOTTED TREES.` → `THE OLD PLANE TREES.`

segments.voice: First, the house and the trees. Seneca opens letter twelve by saying that wherever he turns, he sees signs of his age. The house is crumbling, and he built it. The plane trees are gnarled, their branches twisted and dry, and he planted them himself and saw their first leaves. The manager has been digging and watering. The trees are simply old. So, Seneca realizes, is he. Second, the doorkeeper. Then at the door he sees a frail old man and asks, rather rudely, who on earth that is. The old man answers: don't you know me? I'm Felicio, the son of your old manager. You used to bring me little toys. I was your favorite. Seneca, who wrote this himself, lets the joke land on him. Everything he complains about, he's part of. Third, the turn. And then, instead of sinking, he turns. Let us welcome old age and love it, he says. It's full of pleasure if you know how to use it. Fruit tastes best just as the season ends. Youth is loveliest near its close. The last drink is the one the drinker savors. Every age has its own sweetness, and the late one has a kind all its own. Fourth, together. That's why today's line is we grew old together. Seneca and his trees, Seneca and Felicio, the house and the man who built it. Not a tragedy. A shared life. Something like that may be near you already: a tree in the yard, a friend from school, a mug, a jacket, a street.
screen: `THE HOUSE HE BUILT IS CRUMBLING.` · `FELICIO AT THE DOOR.` · `LOVE OLD AGE; IT HAS ITS SWEETNESS.` · `A SHARED LIFE, NOT A TRAGEDY.` · then, large: `WE GREW OLD TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Look around for something that has aged alongside you. A piece of furniture. A book with a cracked spine. A ring, a photograph, your own hands. If nothing is near, bring one to mind: a tree outside a childhood home, an old friend's face. Look at it carefully, the wear, the softness, the scratches. Notice what it has been through with you. And see whether something like fondness comes, the way it came for Seneca once he stopped scolding. The bell holds the time.
Platanus. Seneca's twelfth letter: the plane tree he planted himself, now gnarled with age, like the house and like him. Today's word.
Your line: we grew old together. Today, notice one thing or one person that has aged with you, and treat it with a little extra care. Day four hundred forty-six.

447.title: Each day a whole life
447.hook: treat each day as if it were a complete life
447.howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism review each evening as if the day were a whole life, tying up what they can, and greet the next morning as a gift.

segments.voice: Yesterday: platanus. Your line was we grew old together. Did you give something or someone that aged with you a little extra care? Day four hundred forty-seven.

Most days don't feel complete. They feel like episodes in a long series: a lot of setup, some unfinished business, and to be continued at the bottom. We go to bed with half the plot still hanging. The second half of Seneca's twelfth letter, the one with the old plane trees, takes that feeling and flips it. What if each day were not an episode, but the whole show? And to make it stick, he tells a very strange story about a Roman governor's dinner parties. Today: each day a whole life.
screen: `TO BE CONTINUED.` → `WHAT IF IT WERE THE WHOLE SHOW?` → `EACH DAY A WHOLE LIFE.`

segments.voice: First, the circles. Seneca says life is made of parts, like circles inside circles. A whole life is the biggest circle. Inside it are the years, the months, and at the center, the smallest circle: a single day. It too has a beginning and an end, a morning and an evening. He quotes the old philosopher Heraclitus: one day is equal to every day. Second, the rule. So, he says, every day should be arranged as if it were the last in the line, as if it rounded off and completed our life. Not in a panic. In order. Third, the strange story. A Roman official named Pacuvius, who governed Syria for years, held a kind of funeral for himself every evening. After dinner, with wine and ceremony, he had himself carried from the table to bed while his servants chanted, in Greek: he has lived, he has lived. Seneca admits Pacuvius did it out of bad habits. But let's do it, he says, from a good conscience. When we go to sleep, let's be able to say gladly: I have lived. Fourth, the gift. And then the best part. If tomorrow comes, Seneca says, take it as a bonus. Whoever can say I have lived, gets up each morning to a gain. This isn't gloom. It's the opposite. A day that's whole doesn't need tomorrow to rescue it. And a tomorrow that arrives anyway is pure gift, unwrapped at sunrise.

segments.voice: Picture tonight, the moment you lie down. Look back over the day as if it were a whole life: a morning, its work, its people, its evening. What would make it feel complete? Not perfect. Complete. Maybe one call made. One thing finished. One thank you said. One apology. Pick one. Picture yourself doing it before evening, and then lying down and saying quietly: I have lived. Breathe with that. The bell holds the time.
Pacuvius. The Roman official who held a nightly funeral for himself, so he could say: I have lived. Today's word.
Your line: a whole life. End today as if it were finished. Do the one thing you picked, and tonight, before sleep, say: I have lived. Day four hundred forty-seven.

448.title: More in imagination
448.hook: we suffer more in imagination than in reality
448.howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism question a fear before acting on it: is it present, is it certain, and is it truly bad?

segments.voice: Yesterday: Pacuvius. Your line was a whole life. Did you lie down last night and say, I have lived? Day four hundred forty-eight. The end of a week.

Your boss sends a message at four forty-five on a Friday: can we talk Monday? That's all. No subject. And by Saturday morning you've lived through the whole meeting a dozen times. You've been criticized, demoted, let go. You've drafted your defense. Then on Monday it turns out she wanted to ask which conference room you like. Two days of suffering for something that never happened. Seneca's thirteenth letter catches this habit in a single sentence. Today: more in imagination.
screen: `CAN WE TALK MONDAY?` → `A WHOLE WEEKEND OF DREAD.` → `MORE IN IMAGINATION.`

segments.voice: First, the line. Seneca tells Lucilius that more things frighten us than actually hurt us. And then, in Gummere's translation: we suffer more often in imagination than in reality. Second, the three mistakes. Some things, Seneca says, torment us more than they should. Some torment us before they should. And some torment us when they shouldn't at all. We exaggerate a trouble, we imagine one that isn't there, or we start suffering it early. Third, the test. So he gives a simple test. When a fear arrives, look at it closely. Is this trouble here now, or still in the future? If it's coming, is it certain, or only likely? And is it really an evil, or does it just feel like one? Much of what we dread, he says, never arrives. Between now and then, a lot can change. Fourth, the week. Look at what Seneca has handed us these seven days: one is enough. All mine is with me. As if seen. Cato. We grew old together. A whole life. And now, more in the mind. One thread runs through them: much of what weighs on us lives in our heads, not in the world, and the world is often kinder than our forecasts. That's not a promise that nothing bad will happen. Seneca had real troubles, and some arrived. It's a habit: check the fear against the facts before you suffer it in full. Often the meeting is about conference rooms.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you're worried about. Let it come in clearly. Now ask Seneca's questions, slowly, one at a time. Is it happening right now, or later? If later, is it certain, or only possible? If it does happen, how bad would it really be, and what could I do? Notice how much of the worry was in the forecast. Then come back to this moment: your breath, your chair, nothing happening yet. The bell holds the time.
Opinione. Seneca's thirteenth letter, in Latin: we suffer more often in opinion than in fact, so check each fear against the facts. Today's word.
Your line: more in the mind. The next time a worry grows today, ask: here now, certain, really bad? Check it against what you actually know. Day four hundred forty-eight.

original.note: Latin: we suffer more often in opinion than in fact, from Seneca's thirteenth letter.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't worry, be happy.
what it means: Seneca says we suffer more in imagination than in reality, and gives a test: is it present, certain, truly bad?
what a scholar hears: the Latin says opinione, by opinion, the same Stoic idea as Epictetus: it's our judgments about things that trouble us.
